chief_complaint: sudden excruciating tearing chest pain radiating to mid-back between shoulder blades accompanied by right arm numbness
hpi_details: 59M with poorly controlled hypertension experiences abrupt onset of agonizing 10/10 'tearing and ripping' anterior chest pain radiating directly through to his thoracic spine between his scapulae. Accompanied by diaphoresis, dizziness, and numbness/weakness in right arm. Arrives in ED looking pale and diaphoretic.
ideas: thinks he is having a massive heart attack and will die instantly
concerns: worried because his right arm feels weak and his blood pressure reading is different in each arm
expectations: wants immediate pain medicine and emergency heart intervention

investigation_events.title: Emergency CT angiography of the aorta
investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency CT angiography report is now available.

results.test: CT angiography of chest and abdomen
results.value: Type A dissection from the ascending aorta through the arch and descending thoracic aorta, involving the brachiocephalic trunk and right coronary ostium

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Type A Aortic Dissection evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Type A Aortic Dissection is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes STAT surgical emergency: immediate cardiothoracic surgery operating room transfer for emergency median sternotomy, ascending aortic replacement with synthetic graft, and aortic valve resuspension/replacement, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden excruciating tearing chest pain radiating to mid-back between shoulder blades accompanied by right arm numbness

Key HPI features: 59M with poorly controlled hypertension experiences abrupt onset of agonizing 10/10 'tearing and ripping' anterior chest pain radiating directly through to his thoracic spine between his scapulae. Accompanied by diaphoresis, dizziness, and numbness/weakness in right arm. Arrives in ED looking pale and diaphoretic.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 112, BP Left Arm 188/104 mmHg, BP Right Arm 132/76 mmHg (significant >20 mmHg inter-arm discrepancy, with the lower pressure on the malperfused right side), RR 24. Palpable right radial pulse markedly weaker than left. Early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation audible at right upper sternal border. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy without acute ST-elevation. STAT CT Angiography (CTA) of chest/abdomen confirms Acute Stanford Type A (DeBakey Type I) Aortic Dissection originating in the ascending aorta just above the sinotubular junction, extending across the aortic arch into the descending thoracic aorta with involvement of the brachiocephalic trunk and right coronary ostium.
Relevant background/PMH: Hypertension for 15 years, Dyslipidemia
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Type A Aortic Dissection.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Blood pressure or pulse difference between the two arms — a hallmark finding.
management_principles: STAT surgical emergency: immediate cardiothoracic surgery operating room transfer for emergency median sternotomy, ascending aortic replacement with synthetic graft, and aortic valve resuspension/replacement
Prior to OR: initiate continuous IV Esmolol infusion to lower heart rate (<60 bpm) and dP/dt FIRST, then add IV Nicardipine/Nitroprusside to lower systolic BP (<120 mmHg)
Place an invasive arterial line in a limb with reliable perfusion, without delaying definitive surgical management
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: sudden excruciating tearing chest pain radiating to mid-back between shoulder blades accompanied by right arm numbness

Palpable right radial pulse markedly weaker than left. Early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation audible at right upper sternal border. reference_soap.assessment: Acute Stanford Type A Aortic Dissection complicated by severe hypertension and right brachiocephalic malperfusion.
reference_soap.plan: STAT surgical emergency: immediate cardiothoracic surgery operating room transfer for emergency median sternotomy, ascending aortic replacement with synthetic graft, and aortic valve resuspension/replacement. Prior to OR: initiate continuous IV Esmolol infusion to lower heart rate (<60 bpm) and dP/dt FIRST, then add IV Nicardipine/Nitroprusside to lower systolic BP (<120 mmHg). Place an invasive arterial line in a limb with reliable perfusion, without delaying definitive surgical management.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical triad of acute aortic dissection (abrupt tearing chest/back pain, pulse/blood pressure deficit, mediastinal widening)
Understand the strict pharmacodynamic rule of beta-blockade (Esmolol) BEFORE vasodilator therapy (Nicardipine) to prevent reflex tachycardia and shear stress (dP/dt)
Classify aortic dissections using Stanford (Type A vs B) and DeBakey systems to guide surgical vs medical management
Outline operative steps and priorities during emergency repair of ascending Type A dissections

teaching.one_liner: A tear in the aortic wall extends through the ascending aorta, causing sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, unequal pulses or blood pressures between arms, and a true surgical emergency.
red_flags: Blood pressure or pulse difference between the two arms — a hallmark finding
Any new neurological symptoms — suggests malperfusion of a major branch artery

must_ask.say: Does the pain feel like tearing or ripping, and does it go straight through to your back?
Did the pain start suddenly, all at once?
Does one arm feel weak or numb compared to the other?
How long have you had high blood pressure, and how controlled has it been?
Have you felt sweaty or dizzy?

history.answer: Doctor, please help me! I suddenly got this unbearable, tearing pain in my chest and back about two hours ago, and my right arm feels numb.
It started completely out of the blue about two hours ago while I was sitting in my truck taking a break.
The pain is right in the center of my chest behind my breastbone, and it goes straight through to the center of my upper back.
It feels like something is literally ripping and tearing open inside my chest.
Yes, it shoots straight through from my chest into my back, right between my shoulder blades.
It reached maximum agonizing intensity the instant it started, and it has stayed constant without letting up for two hours.
It is definitely a ten out of ten; this is the worst, most agonizing pain I have ever experienced.
Resting hasn't helped at all; it started while I was sitting down, and nothing I do makes it feel any better.
Taking a deep breath, coughing, or changing my posture does not change the pain at all.
No, it is not related to eating, and I haven't had any heartburn, acid reflux, or difficulty swallowing.
Yes, I broke out in a heavy cold sweat immediately, and I've been feeling dizzy and lightheaded since the pain hit.
I feel short of breath because the pain is so intense, and a bit nauseous, but I haven't vomited.
Right when the chest pain started, my right arm went numb, tingling, and felt weak.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, cough, or phlegm.
No, I haven't had any cold, flu, sore throat, or illness recently.
No, neither of my legs is swollen or painful, and I haven't had any surgery, long flights, or bed rest.
No, there are no rashes, blisters, or skin changes anywhere on my chest or back.
I am terrified that I am having a massive heart attack and that I'm going to die right here.
The triage nurse said my blood pressure was much lower in my right arm than my left, and that really frightens me.
No, I have never felt anything like this pain before in my life.
I have never had any heart tests, angiograms, or stents placed.
No, I haven't had any falls, car accidents, chest trauma, or heavy lifting.
I have had high blood pressure for about fifteen years, and my doctor told me I also have high cholesterol.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am prescribed amlodipine ten milligrams once a day for my blood pressure, but I often forget to take it.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have smoked about a pack of cigarettes a day for forty years.
I might drink a beer or two on weekends when I'm not driving my truck, but nothing heavy.
I work as a long-haul truck driver and live at home with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke in his sixties; no one had heart attacks or aneurysms that I know of.
I need something strong to stop this terrible pain right now, and I need emergency treatment to fix my heart.

exam.finding: The patient appears acutely distressed, pale, and profusely diaphoretic, clutching his chest.

Blood pressure is 188/104 mmHg in the left arm and 132/76 mmHg in the right arm; heart rate is 112 bpm, respiratory rate is 24 breaths/min, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and temperature is 36.8°C.
No jugular venous distension noted; internal jugular venous pulsation is not elevated.
No chest wall deformity, ecchymosis, or reproducible tenderness on palpation of the sternum, ribs, or costochondral junctions.
Resonant to percussion bilaterally with symmetric diaphragmatic excursion.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with symmetric air entry and no wheezes, crackles, or pleural friction rubs.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with an early diastolic decrescendo murmur audible at the right upper sternal border; no gallop or pericardial friction rub.
Right radial pulse is markedly diminished and weak compared to a bounding left radial pulse; femoral and posterior tibial pulses are intact bilaterally.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender without guarding, rigidity, or palpable pulsatile masses.
Calves are symmetric, non-swollen, and non-tender bilaterally with negative Homan sign; no lower extremity edema.
Motor strength is reduced to 4/5 in the right upper extremity, but 5/5 in the left upper extremity and both lower extremities.
Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick throughout the right upper extremity, with intact sensation in all other limbs.
